blocks.x: Okay, it's going. Do you want to give your name first? Well, my name is Jasper Taylor. Is Jasper where you're born?
In Texarkana, Arkansas, and Texas.
The town right there on the border, isn't it?
Right there on the border.
Can you give us the birth date?
January the 1st, 1894.
And you remember the very first music you heard?

Well, the very first music I heard was about my mother. She used to play the organ, the old-fashioned foot organ, and later on we bought a flat-top piano. And I always heard my mother play the hymns from the church books. And that's, I got my inspiration from my mother, I guess.
Anyone else in the family? Do you have any older brothers?
No, no. I had a sister. She passed when she was a child.
I remember that Scott Joplin, I think, came from there, who wrote all the ragtime. Did you ever hear him when you were young or know anything about him down there?

I didn't. I used to see him, and I knew his family very well. I went to school with S.A.D. Joplin. Oh, a relative. A relative. And I know Willie had turned time. He later on, he married S.A.D., and he played the trombone. And only later on I became more acquainted with Joplin's works by playing the Maple Leaf Rag and other tunes that he wrote.
Now, when did you take up music? What was your first instrument and so on?
Oh, drums. I used to play the drums in the backyard and on the fences and down in the barn.
Did you just hit on anything?
Oh, anything. Mostly a bucket, tin tub.
What kind of sticks did you have?
Oh, I had sticks, homemade sticks made from chairs, wooden chairs, and I could always somehow beat rhythm with those sticks.
Did you play with any other kids with music and other instruments?
Oh, we had our tin can bands, yes.
Did you have any lessons on drums or any other instruments when you were a boy?
No, music lessons. No, I didn't have them until I joined the school band.
About when was that? How old?
Oh, I don't know about, I don't know. I was in an industrial school and they had a band. Yeah. And then I finally worked myself up on the drums. You had a real drum set then.
Yeah. What kind of a set did you get at first? How many?
Well, the first I just had one drum for the military band.
Did you play bass drum or snare? Snare drum.
Yeah. And I only, when I played the set of drums with the piano player for dances, so I started.

Do you remember any of the danced orchestras or bands around? What kind of music they played? What? How big the bands were? What kind of a band? What kind of music? If it was ragtime or waltzes or what kind of music they played?

Oh, well, I heard several of the bands. The best bands I heard before I went out on my own was the mysterious mistral bands, such as the Rabbit Foot, A.G. Allen Mistral, and, uh, The Dandy Dixie Mistral, The Georgia Mistral, The Algae Fields, The Blue Dock Stata. I heard it all about that.
Um, how late, uh, how long did you stay in Texarkana?
Oh, I stayed there until about 1912.
What was your first job? Did you play any music professionally? That is, did you get along to any band there before you left?
No, I used to play with the piano player, play dances.
You did play dances, though, before you left? Yeah. Excellent. Do you remember who the piano player was? What kind of music did you know?

I just can't, she was a woman, I just can't think of her name now, but she was the hottest piano player around town, and we played generally all the little dances, little Saturday night get-togethers. For 75 cents a dollar and a half, or anything like that.

Do you remember when you were a boy in New Orleans that some of the people say that the piano was considered sort of a sissy instrument and most of the boys wouldn't take up piano? Was that true in your hometown, do you think, the reason this girl, good pianist, the boys didn't take it up or not?
Well, that's right, the boys didn't go for the piano much. They wanted the horns, brass horns, playinets, and so forth.
After you left Texarkana, can you tell us what you did next?

Well, I went out on a circus, and it was a Wild West show, I called it a circus. Young Buffalo Bill Wild West. I knew a man over there and I just went out for the summer months. And I would always go back home to school. It wasn't a month.
Was that a regular brass band?
That's how I really got started, professionally.
Was that a regular brass band?
Regular brass band on a side shore. They had a minstrel in the band.
Well, did you have to parade any to advertise the show to, or?
Well, they paraded every day in every town that we visited. The band would parade on a wagon. They had a special bandwagon those days.
Do you remember what kind of music they used? Were they all marches, or did you play some ragtime pieces and blues or anything ever like that? That is, that it would be called ragtime or jazz?
Well, in 1911, all I played was the marches and the ragtime tunes. And I don't recall any blues, only just a makeup blues. Some trombone player had. And a band like that, there was lack of blues.
Yeah. And after you left the circus, where did you go next, and what was your next experience?
Well, I went out with it in 19... 1912. And for... and stayed with the... stayed with the sex until it closed. And I joined the Dandy Dixie Minstrels as a drummer for band and orchestra.
Did they travel all around the South in the wintertime too, or just in the summer?
In the winter and summer. I... I quit the circus in somewhere around October, and I joined the minstrel show in Mexico. And we toured Mexico and Texas on the 10th, the Dandy Dixie Minstrels.
How long did you stay with...

Well, I stayed with the Dandy Dixie Minstrels for several months, and that's why I began to study the drums, the xylophone, very, very much. And I bumped with the trumpet player, and he was a professor. He played the violin and the... the... Carnet. And he began to teach me the seriousness of music, and...
Do you remember his name, or where he came from?
His name was Wilson, the last name. He was from... Sir Wickley, Pennsylvania.
Way over there.

And he... And he... I bought a set of bells, and I used to play the violin parts on the orchestra bells, and later on I bought xylophones. And he taught me to read... And so well that I could read mostly anything written.

And I know Baby Dobbs once told me that you were the only really Finnish drummer in Chicago, he thought. That is, that you were a wonderful musician, could read, and you could play all of the different instruments. Xylophone, of course, seems Baby never learned some of those other instruments like the bells. And so he always told me about you were really what he called a Finnish drummer. And you didn't have any special instruction on the bells, except just learning to read that time, or did...
Professor Wilson.
He did show you how to... he could play the bells and xylophone too.

That's right. I had... They had some... I had some books on... on hammering. I had some books on the other hand. I had some books on the other hand. I had some books on the other hand. I had some books on the other hand. I had some books on the other hand. But I used to take those difficult violin instructors and play everything in there. As written.
Can you tell us the next band you joined, or show, whatever it was?

Well, the next band, I... We went into Memphis. We went back for a little vacation, a couple of weeks. And while I was in Memphis, I went up on Beale Street, and I saw a sign in a nightclub like this, stuff snare drum was split. He couldn't use it. And so he was, didn't know what to do and I stepped up and gave him my card with my name on it. I was very proud of that card, Jasper Taylor, drums, bells, xylophone and Dandy Dixie Minstrels. And he said, well where is your drum? I told him it was on the car at the station. This was a railroad show. We had two cars, a baggage car and a car for sleeping. So we made a deal and I went down and got my drum and brought it back up. And so he played a few pieces and I, on the inside of me, told me that I could, was a better drummer than this young man. And it wasn't long before he extended me an invitation to play a tune. And this tune that they played was a tune that the musical band was playing. And I was right at home and then he got out the drum parts to, had bells, a lot of bells, a lot of bell work. And he wanted to see if I could play the bells as I stated on my business card.
Yes.
And so they were very well pleased.
What was the name of that band again?
Eckford's band of Memphis.
Did you meet Handy up there in Memphis soon?

Well, the news seemed to spread all over. The next day the boys made me very welcome and told me to go get my clothes and leave the musical show. They were going to get me with a band. And this drummer was drumming in the Metropolitan Theater and carrying me. His name was Mr. Baker. And I'll never forget him. And so he he split his work with me. He let me play in the theater and I played the shows. And I knew show business because I was playing a big menstrual show that had bottom legs.
About what year was that? Can you remember?
That was around, I think it was in Part 12 and Part 18.
That early, right before the First World War.

Yeah. And so the next day I met Handy, and I was recommended, and Handy told me to, at that time he was operating what they called a syndicate, Handy syndicate, employing almost 100 musicians. He had dance work in the state of Arkansas, Texas, Mississippi, and went as far as Louisiana. Dance work, he was sending musicians down in groups, all the way from piano and drums to seven-piece combinations, eight-piece combinations, and highest 15. He also had the 400, the fashionable 400 work there.
Had he written many of his pieces at that time, the Memphis Blues, do you remember that? St. Louis Blues, was that out at that time?
Well, that St. Louis, if I can remember the St. Louis Blues, I was with him when he wrote the St. Louis Blues, and that was something around 14.
That's right, I think, I believe I remember, the copyright, I think, was about a little later than the Memphis Blues.
Yeah.

Do you remember, did any New Orleans bands ever get up to Memphis in those years on votes or any other way, any other single musicians, piano players, or anybody else, like Jelly Roll Martin or anybody up in there?
Yes, in fact, in the combination, Handy had George Williams.
Oh, that's right, was he from New Orleans? I knew the fellas talk about him down there.
Yeah, he was a great...
Like Roy Palmer said he inspired him.

He was a great trombonist, and he was, did all the trombone work for the, for the Handis Syndicate, and we had another one in the Syndicate. His name was Higgins, the banjo. He played banjo and sang, and then we, another New Orleans man we had was Walls, the great bass player.
Archie Walls.

Archie Walls. Archie Walls, born and raised. And there, and there were others that I can't recall, but we had many, many New Orleans musicians were playing with Handis Syndicate, played such as, as I said, out in society, fashionable society. And we went on the plantations down in the Delta. And there were, Saturdays, I guess there was at least a hundred men out. Yeah. That's, uh... I happened to stay there.
What kind of music did you play? Do you remember some of the numbers? Were they ragtime, blues, the popular tunes of the day, or waltzes? What type of...

Well, I remember that there was competition. There was another band by the name of Bynum's Band, Handis Band, as I told you, Egford's Band, and the Big Six from, from Big Sprague, Mississippi. They were in that territory. And it was a matter of competition, and, uh, Handis' biggest competitor was, uh, the Bynum Band, and they had, uh, Jeff Clark on piano, on trumpet, Elick Valentine on trombone.
Well, I think of it, uh, to change the subject, uh, did Johnny Dunn come from Memphis? Do you remember him?
Johnny Dunn came from Memphis. His father ran a clothing store on Beale Street.
Was he playing around when you went there?
Well, he was...
Do you remember him, or had he left?
Oh, he was a kid, playing in the Metropolitan Theater, just part-time. See, I never knew him.
Taking lessons from Charlie Williamson. Was he younger than you, do you think, or about the same age?
Oh, he was younger, much younger. Oh, I didn't know.
Much younger.

Much younger. And then, uh, uh, the, uh, uh, and, uh, why, uh, Handy, uh, uh, what inspired Handy to write, uh, Mr. Crump, which later was, uh, changed and called Memphis Blues, was because Jeff Smith wrote a number called, uh, The Beale Street Squabble. And, uh, this number was a big hit, and in those days they paraded around in, uh, wagons and trucks with the bed. Yeah. And, uh, Handy wrote Mr. Crump and Jeff, to, to answer Jeff Smith's Beale Street Squabble. And then there, there, and then there, they began writing various waltzes. And, uh, finally they fell into the, more of the blues. Each band had a blues of its own.

By the way, do you remember in any of your early days, any parades? Like in New Orleans, they used brass bands for funerals, too. You know, they still used those. They'll have the band out for a funeral. Did you ever?
I, I didn't, I didn't, I didn't, they didn't have that in Memphis. As I can remember, that was only happened in New Orleans.
But I wondered any other, or Texas, you don't remember ever any bands, funerals, that way?
Only when I came to Chicago, I played a few films with the band.
When did you come to Chicago? Yeah, in my... I don't want to skip over the rest of your life, you went over to Europe, too, didn't you? In the Army or something? In the Army, yeah.
I came to Chicago in 1917 for the purpose of opening up the Owl Theater to play drums in the Owl Theater. They were building it.
Where was that on State?
47th and State. Clarence Jones was the orchestra leader.
Do you remember who else was in that band then?
In the, uh, Owl Theater band? Oh, yes. Arthur Hill on trombone. And, uh, I did, uh, White Houston on the violin. And that's all I can recall now.
Were there any New Orleans fellows by any chance, you think, in that band? Or do you remember the first New Orleans musicians you met or heard up here?

Uh, oh, many, many in Chicago. But, uh, I would like to make the statement that, uh, before I came to Chicago, I met, uh, Piran, the violinist, and Clarence William, the pianist. They made a tour to Memphis, from New Orleans to Memphis. And they were pushing a song that they wrote called, uh, I Can Beat You Doing What You're Doing Me. And they made a tour with a handy band as a team from New Orleans. Clarence sang and played the piano. Piran played the violin. And they were playing the violin, and what a violin he could play. And we toured with the Mississippi, Arkansas, and, and parts of Louisiana. And there were another great musician from New Orleans by the name of William King Phillips. Of course, he came from Florida, New Orleans, Memphis. Yeah. And he could do great things on the clarinet, such as T.O. And he was a great admirer of T.O.
When did you first hear or meet T.O.?
I met, uh, I didn't hear T.O. until I came to Chicago. He came up with the first New Orleans Creole band. Uh, that is, uh, the first one I knew about. Yeah, the first one you knew about.
Do you remember who else was in the band? Any of the other fellows?
Yes, uh, Armand, uh, P.R.E.S. T.O. on clarinet, and Eddie Adkins on trombone. And, uh, what's the drummer's name? You know about that, huh?
Is it old man Contrell, they call him?
That's Contrell.

It really should be Contrell. They usually call it Contrell. That's it, Contrell. He wasn't old in those days, but he has a son now, so they usually speak of him as old man Contrell. Contrell. Uh, Baby took a few lessons from him. Natty Dominick started as a drummer with a few lessons from Contrell.

That's so. He was a good drummer. A good, solid, good, solid beat. Good right and left hand. And, uh, when I heard that band, I, uh, I, I'll tell you, I was so excited I couldn't sleep. It was the greatest.
Was it different than the other Chicago bands?

Oh, my goodness. King Phillips, William King Phillips, is the one, uh, that, uh, uh, to take me to hear this band. They gave, just, they just gave a kind of a free concert for all Chicago musicians to come and listen to the Dixieland style of music, which we had never heard. And, of course, you know the history tells us that, uh, everybody went wild. All the musicians started drumming.
Was it much different style than, uh, the Memphis music that you'd heard down there and been playing?
Oh, no, we didn't play nothing like that, uh, like the New Orleans, uh, style of music in Memphis. No, sir. Only, only the slow numbers, like the blues.
The blues would be pretty much the same anyplace then?
Pretty much, uh-uh, especially when you play them medium or slow.

Oh, yeah. Uh, can you think of anything else to explain? Uh, I know it's a little difficult to explain in words just about music, but, uh, what else excited you about this band? I know you would be watching the drummer, but, uh, anything else in particular about the style of it? The clarinet, trumpet, or trombone, anything different?

Well, I noticed that the, uh, uh, we were playing at that time, uh, more on a centipated beat and ragtime. And, of course, I played a lot of, uh, semi-classics and classics. And in those days you, uh, classed, uh, if you couldn't play the classics, you wasn't counted for much. Well, these, uh, these boys, they come, come here with this new beat and the clarinets, to me, seems, that blew the tunes, the trumpets, uh, uh, uh, just something that's new I can't explain. I understand. Just, uh, and everybody got with it around Chicago. It became the rage. They call it, uh, Dixieland, and then later on they call it, uh, jazz, and later on...

Okay, it's going, we were talking about the New Orleans bands when they first hit Chicago. Did they, did you notice anything special about the tempo? Did they play slower numbers more than the Chicago bands, or mix them up, or...?

Well, uh, more, well they had, uh, their music was, uh, more on a medium beat. Most of their tunes were just, uh, what you might say, uh, medium two. It's their best tunes, such as the Weary Blues. And I don't know, Arty Matthews wrote Weary Blues, but, uh, they, uh, I don't know why they had it down. They had it down there.

They always call that Shake It and Break It. They still do down there. They speak of it, they have the words they sing about Shake It and Break It, hang it on the wall. So they still call that tune the Shake It and Break It quite often.

Now here's something that is important, very important, uh, I think, uh, I've often asked myself, where did Handy get the Spanish beat in St. Louis Blues? Yeah, I know what you mean. I often wondered why he, why, why, why, then Robert Campbell told me last week that Handy was in Cuba with the Meharry Mestrels. And that Lucille Handy, his oldest daughter was, I, he said that, uh, was born in Cuba. I never heard Handy say that out of the years that I was associated with him. But Robert Campbell, who was closer than I, and he played. And if you like stuff

trumpet for Handy back in those days, and as a great Handy fan, and before Handy passed, he called him in to be a witness on his will. And I saw him in the hospital here last week, and he gave me that information, which I did not know. That Handy was the leader of the new ones, and Harry Mestrels, and they went to Cuba in 1906 or something like that. So we, so I just, it's just an idea of mine, and probably he got that beat from over there.

Gave him that idea. Were there many new different tunes that you hadn't heard before the New Orleans fellas played? What they call today like the Dixieland numbers, you know, those things like Tiger Rag and all those. Did they play many of those?

No, we didn't hear anything about Tiger Rag until the, came from New Orleans, and the Liver Stable Blues, and Blue in the Blues, and the Freddie Kippert's Blues. And incidentally, Freddie Kippert was freelancing around Chicago for a long time.
When did you first meet him or hear him?

Well, I met Freddie at, well, I was playing at the Owl Theater, and at nights I would go down on the Strobe, we call it, around the Asia Cafe, and you could meet mostly anyone there. That was a hangout, the Chinese restaurant.
What cafe was it?
Uh, what did I say that was, Brian? Asia Cafe. Asia Cafe. Yeah, Asia Cafe at 35th and State. Asia, A-S-I-E. Oh, yeah.
Asia.

Asia. Asia. Chinese restaurant. And I met Freddie there. And then, at that time you had, that was a stroll, we had the stroll, and there was a place of entertainment, two and three in a block. And you just walked from 31st to 35th, and you go in mostly the, any of the places of entertainment, they had a band there.
Trevor Compton was telling me about the E-Light number one, number two, and the Deluxe, and Dreamland were all along there. Yeah. Did you play those places too, or mostly just the theaters? Theaters.
Theaters. Mm-hmm. And after, after our places I also would play there. Yeah.

Yeah. Uh, while we're thinking of Keppard, I did want to ask a good deal about that, about him, because you made the only record that his name was ever on the label, Freddie Keppard, the Stockyard and the Salty Dog. Yes. You were on that date. And then the other record was made about the same time, the one under your name.
Yeah, well, Stockyard Blues, that's mine. I just simply had my, played over on the Zillophone and Freddie, got the boys together. And, you know, it didn't take very long before they fall in. Yes.
Can you remember who else was on the date?
Well, uh, let me see, I know Camel was on piano, and, uh, I know the, the trombone player, but I just can't call his name just now. I'm trying to think too, but that's-
Vinson.
Vinson. Yes, Vinson, he was on the.
The clarinet, um-
It was about a twelve piece band.
Was it that big? Yeah. How do you know it was that big?
Oh, yeah. We had, uh, see there's about that, quite a few on the basses.
I think we played that record for you up at John Steiner's, oh, several years ago when I was living up there. And if I remember rightly, you identified Johnny Dodds as the clarinetist.
Yeah. And then we had, uh, now we're playing the wood blocks.
Yeah. Uh, did you play washboard on any of that date, or either one of those? No, no, no.
I only played, uh, washboard with, uh, James O'Brien's trio, washboard trio.
When did you start with those washboards? After you hit Chicago, that kind of music? No. Or have you ever played that in the minstrel days, too, or?

No, I got that the same time I started a slapstick. I used to do a slapstick on, uh, on the Handy Band, on Memphis Blues. Like you see them all applaud, I mean, uh, clap hands. Yeah, on the offbeat? Yeah, well I, I, uh, was on a wood pile down in Mississippi. We were on a date down there. And I stopped by this wood pile and I picked up an old washboard and I picked up, uh, two, uh, flat boards. And I put a leather on one end. I said, this guy, they came to me and said, instead of clapping my hand, I'm gonna clap this board tonight. And it went over big. And, uh, and I started fooling around with the washboard from then on. Trying to, I saw a man play fish pools. You know the material made out of fish pools? Yeah, all the bamboo.
Yeah.

He had a, had a, several of them put together and I saw him strumming them like, and blowing a whistle. Uh, not a whistle, blowing a mouth organ. Yeah. And keeping rhythm with this cane, made of cane. And so I, I just did the same thing with the washboard.
Yeah.

That's where I started. And then finally I, I could, uh, do some acrobatic tricks with the washboard. Which it did as much as, it was entertaining, very entertaining. Right. Which I can't do today. I could carry a washboard spinning around under my legs and over my shoulder. Oh yeah. Like that.
I never saw that.
Yeah.

Uh, is there anything else you could tell us about that one record date? The, uh, two sides that are under your name are made, must have been made about the same day or if you remember if it was the next day, it was pretty close together, I think, according to the number on the record.

Uh, well I think they, they, those were made on one date. On one date, you think? Yeah. That's right. And I would like to, while we're talking about it, I would like to, we'll bring in Jell-A-Roll Morton.
Oh yes, I'd like for you to tell us.

Yeah, well I knew, I first met Jell-A-Roll Morton down in Memphis. And, uh, he came into Memphis as the world's greatest piano player. And I guess I was about to, one of the first to, to hear him. He had a blues, Jell-A-Roll blues. This was after Handy had published his blues. And Jell-A-Roll gave a regular concert for him and I and, uh, a couple of ladies. And that's how I first met Jell-A-Roll. And then I went out on some jobs with him, piano and drums, in Memphis. And then we came, then I came to Chicago and, uh, Jell-A-Roll went back to New Orleans. And, uh, then he came up to Chicago. And I think I made one of the first records with him, uh, Jeanette.
Oh, you made that Jeanette?
I think Jeanette was going there.
Mr. Jell-A-Lord, I believe is one of you.
And he told me I'm the first drummer to ever play a drum solo on a record. And he said it was with his band, but I don't, I never heard that solo. You don't remember? I don't remember.
How did he play piano when you first heard him say in Memphis? Was he really good then?

I liked him of course. Oh, wonderful. Good, good, uh, good. I liked that leaping bass he played. Oh, he was a wonderful piano player. He just amazed you when he first sat down. As we call it in the music world, he had some quips that wouldn't do.
Was he fairly easy to get along with or difficult, would you say? Some people say one and some of the others.

Well, Jell-A-Roll, uh, I got along with him. First, he was a sporting type of young fella, good looking to me, dressed well, had a diamond in his tube. And I always groomed his hair, had an automobile and a big yellow dog. And he was boastful. He was a great piano player. He says, I am great, and I know it, and he was great.
That's what I always thought too.

Yeah. I always thought of that. And he could do many, many, many things on the piano. And I think that he was the first to start what we call in music, riffs. And that first tune that he wrote, what was it? King Porter. King Porter, King Porter. If you see the piano part of King Porter, you'll see your first riffs. King Porter. And, uh, I don't know. That was when I heard him in Chicago. I didn't hear him. I don't know whether he got that from some of the bands in the South or not. But, uh, Jell-O Roll has always been around. Hillman, who knew him in New Orleans, uh, they played together. And they said he always played as a single, by himself mostly.
Did you ever work with him in a band up here? Yes, I have. Aside from the record that you made.
Yes, I played, played, uh, played with, uh, Jell-O Roll many times on dances, dance dates. It always went over big. Sensational.
I understood he had a band sometimes that go out of town and travel. Did you ever travel on any tour with him?

No, I didn't travel on any tour. Just around town. He would get a lot of dates himself. A lot of dance dates and pick his musicians. And every time he could, uh, cause I were, uh, the earlier part of the nights, generally I were, uh, in the theater. If there's any way that he could wake me in on the date. Uh, if it run late, well, he would do so. Uh huh.

Of other New Orleans, uh, drummers, do you remember any, uh, others you mentioned, Cottrell, who first came up. Do you remember any of the other bands that came up like when Joe Oliver's band first came up?

Oh, yeah. I know about Jimmy Nooney, when he first came up. And, uh, I think he was with the Joe Oliver band for a while. And then he had a band of his own very shortly after that. And then, uh, I had some wonderful drummers. Uh, Baby Hall was, uh, New Orleans drummer. And he had, he's one that had a great reputation for holding the time very steady. Uh, if he knocked off at a certain tempo, the beginning of that tempo was the same at the ending of the piece as it was in the beginning. Uh, and he, the five-stroke, uh, beat was one of his, uh, best beats. Five-stroke roll. Is that a sort of a press roll? No, it wasn't a press. It was legitimate. Now, Baby Dodds was known for the press. And, uh, it, it was really a press. And it was musical and I don't know. The nearest man to the press roll, uh, to Baby Dodds was, uh, Sudie. Oh, yeah. Sudie Samson. He could do it very near, but he couldn't, he couldn't do it like Baby Dodds.

I know Baby was famous for that press roll. I used to ask him to try to explain it a little, how he did it. And he, he would never, he could show you, but he wouldn't put it in words. Can you tell a little bit? What do you do? Just sort of drag your stick across the drum?

Uh, Baby, Baby, it was a rebound. In drumming, we have a first, one of the first things you learn to bounce your stick. You could just raise it up on the drum and drop it and just hold it loose. And it will, uh, uh, uh, it will, uh, you'll get what they call a rebound.
Yes, I understand.
Uh-huh. Yeah, rebouncing. And, uh, Baby had a way that, uh, he could, uh, pause or rebound, pulling rebound. It would give it, it would just give a zzzz, zzzz, and, uh, he could control.
Just throw the stick on once and then sort of draw it.
Yeah, and draw, draw it, draw it twice.
And keep on bouncing.
Yeah, and keep on bouncing. Yeah. Which is a very difficult thing to do. And I never seen anyone that could do it as well as Baby.
Did both, do both hands do that? Or just the one hand?
Both hands, both hands.
Both of them are bouncing at the same time. That's right. So it may be one bounce and then if you...
the beat, but you give him another beat with the other hand.
I've tried to do it. I tried to get him to show me, and he'd show me with the same thing.
Yeah, I know what you mean.

And another thing about it, I think that a drummer must have what I call, he must feel the beat, feeling the beat. You can always tell a drummer when he feels the beat. Baby Dodds was a man who felt the beat. His whole body responded to the rhythms. He would shimmy and rock and both feet going and press by, and it was just wonderful to watch.
He always seemed so happy. Always had that smile on his face.

And everything was his own. It came out of his own head. I don't think he patterned after anyone. And I used to tell him I'm going to have a lot of fun with him, and I told him I was going to make a musical bed spring. He said, well let me see it. And there was, Baby Hall was a famous five-stroke old man. He did it perfect. He was a good timekeeper, and I think that his, he was another one who could feel the beat. I believe Zutty could feel the beat. He just got to feel it. I've seen a lot of great drummers who were just, had a great technique on the drums, and could do many tricks, and all sorts of rhythm, but they just couldn't feel the beat. They just, they just play along with the band, but they never could excite anyone. And I think that I can feel the beat a little bit, but not much as Baby Hall.
I'm sure you can. Baby admired you, I know, a lot. He told me that several times.
And I want to give a lot of credit to Gene Cooper. That's another boy can feel the beat. I think it goes all over.
Well, I was going to ask you a little bit about Jimmy Bertrand. I know he didn't come from New Orleans, and I've never talked to him. Do you know where he came from? Is he from Chicago, native here?
Well, Bertrand, I think the family. I think he didn't, I think he was from New Orleans. I thought they might have come down. Bertrand, yeah, yeah, we're French.
I'd name it.
Well, I think he was in Memphis. But his music started in Chicago professionally.
Did he really specialize on washboards? He played that sometime too?

No, he could play it, but Jimmy was an exceptional drummer, a good school drummer. He studied with Russick of the Tivoli Theater, a big 50-piece band out there. Russick played the timpani. I know I studied with him, studied drums with him. Jimmy took Zillophone and Tiffany from Russick. He studied with straight and many other drummers that I had. Two or three more are good top drummers I know that he studied with. And he had a very good left hand and a very good right hand. And he could read music. And he played the Zillophone better than anyone at that time.
I never got to hear him in person or meet him. Is he still living, do you think?
Yes, he is living. But he's not drumming.

That's what I understand. Are there any of the other New Orleans musicians? I keep sort of bringing you back to that. I'm not trying to make you talk about only them, but I wondered any other fellows that you could talk about from New Orleans or do you remember the other musicians that you might have worked with?
Well, I think that Jimmy Noon was a great musician. I think, if I make no mistake, I think he wrote Sweet Lorraine.
That was his theme song anyway, I'm sure.

Sweet Lorraine is one of the great romantic stories, love stories. And I knew Jimmy Noonan. And I know he loved his wife. I think his wife's name was Lorraine. Sweet Lorraine. And every time I hear that number, I think of Jimmy Noonan.
I think everybody does.
He was a lovely fellow.
He was, yeah.

Never did anything to hate the feelings of anyone. And he was with Lorraine, Sweet Lorraine when he passed. And I look upon Sweet Lorraine as one of the great classics. But every time I hear it, it touches me. Because I knew how he loved, loved his wife, how devoted he was. I never even knew of Jimmy, even smiling at another female. He was that devoted. And if you just listen to the words of Sweet Lorraine, you can almost feel it yourself.
Speaking of New Orleans, did you ever get there to work there or go down?
Well, I was getting through there with the Wild West show. I was sitting up on a bandwagon. But I never did go down there on a date.
Did you hear any music there at all when you went through?
No, I did not.
Sort of rode through.

Yeah, just rode through. But I was born and raised 30 miles from Sweet Sport, Louisiana. And I played with many Louisiana musicians from Alexandria, Louisiana, and Sweet Sport, Louisiana, and other points in Louisiana. And all of them, to me, had good rhythms and good perception of music.

We only have another minute or so on here. I wonder if you have anything to add to what you said about Freddie Kepard. Since he's not here anymore to talk for himself, do you remember about his tone and style? Of course, we can hear it on the record, but a lot of people say he sounded much better than that, even.

But, yes, Freddie Kepard was a great outside man, we would call him. I know that the story of him, Tim Brim in New York, that the Coconut Grove had a band, a great band over there, something like 15 pieces. And he wanted, he kept hearing about this New Orleans style of music. So Freddie Kepard told me. So Freddie showed me the telegram that Tim Brim wanted him to come immediately, to join him at the Coconut Grove in New York. And Freddie was in love with Chicago. And so he went over to New York, and the story is, out that he just went over big in New York at the Coconut Grove. That was a spot for society dancers. They said they never heard such music. And he played what you call on the outside of the band. They would just do an organ or some sort of a beat or riff behind his work, and he could take that derby and do wonders.
Just be featured by himself.
Featured by himself with the band behind him. That's all he did.
Would that be for a whole number or just a certain chorus?

Just parts of the numbers. Yeah. And Freddie Kepard, I think, could blow at something louder than any man I ever heard. Do you remember? He could blow above the band. The band would be just blowing what we call a double F, double F-Z. And Freddie Kepard must have been five Zs, because he was above, you could hear him above the band. And he, one peculiarity he had, he weighed about 275 or something, approaching 300. And he liked his fresh refreshments. And that was all in the contract. He would set it down by the pitcher. And he would just sip and blow.
Do you remember if he would read music much, ever use arrangements, or mostly just from his head and by ear?
Yes, Freddie could read music. He could, he could read music.
Like the record, didn't you?
But generally, generally, he prefer improvising. Yeah.
On the records you made, were any of those things written out, or just all, and you taught them that tune?
Well, just the, just the, what we call head, all from the middle.
I think it's just about through here. There's something else you want to add. I think that covered the, you've already installed it pretty well.
Well, the only thing that I would like to add, that I'm proud of you. Thank you.
